Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:123: Therefore I say that whoever has no rooster should find himself a companion who does not sleep until midnight, in order to wake him precisely at midnight; and his companion has a reward, as is written regarding David and his men (I Samuel 30:24), "for as his share is who goes down to battle, so shall his share be who stays by the baggage; they shall share alike" — and they should alternate. Or [he could have] a craftsman who does not mind the matter [of staying up]. And if he is in a place where none of the aforementioned arrangements are available, it is fitting that he not lie down on a made-up bed, and not undress his whole body. And I have heard that the sage, the honorable Rabbi Yosef Taitatzak, peace be upon him, for seventy years did not sleep on a made-up bed except from Sabbath to Sabbath, and it is said that his practice was to sleep upon a single chest with his legs hanging, and he would rise precisely at midnight, and no one knew of this until after his death, when his wife told of it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:124: It is fitting to swear and vow to fulfill these arrangements, for we find that King David, peace be upon him, swore and vowed regarding something similar, as it is said, "who swore to the Lord, vowed to the Mighty One of Jacob: Surely I will not come into the tent of my house, nor go up into my bed; I will not give sleep to my eyes, or slumber to my eyelids..." (Psalms 132:2-4). Nevertheless, one should swear only to something he estimates he can fulfill. We have written regarding the conditions of vows and oaths below, in chapter 14 — see there. Likewise it is fitting to vow not to overindulge in eating and drinking beyond a measure he knows will not increase his sleep.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:125: If he prepares a rooster, he should try to have it be black, which is more precisely aligned than others, as is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayechi 218b), in these words: and therefore, at precisely midnight, when the spirit from the north side is aroused, one flame goes forth and strikes beneath the wings of the rooster and it crows, and all the more so with a black rooster, which is more precisely aligned than another — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:126: Also, one who is not accustomed to fasting and does not rise at midnight, it is good for him to eat during the day, at least an hour before nightfall, so that there be time for the food to be digested and his sleep not increase when he rises at midnight; and he should conduct himself thus for a while until he becomes established in this practice, particularly during the summer months when the nights are short.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:127: Also, it is fitting that he train himself to sleep in some of his clothes, and not sleep naked between the sheets, for it will be difficult for him to rise, particularly in the cold. This is the quality of alacrity — that he be zealous before he comes to a stumbling block — for they said (Avot 6:4), "this is the way of Torah: sleep on the ground," the reason being that he should suffer discomfort and not find his body at rest, so that he not come to sleep the whole night — so Rabbi Yosef Yavetz, peace be upon him, explains. And at the very least, if he does not have the strength to sleep on the ground, he should not indulge in sleeping on a made-up bed with sheets. All this is fitting for one who wishes to repent, to rectify the rest of his nights, and not have demanded of him an account of the many nights he wasted in sleep and idleness.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:128: According to the words of the Zohar, a person is always obligated to rise to occupy himself with Torah at night, whether in the rainy season or in the summer, for they said (Parashat Bereshit 4a), "Who does not await this every day?" as we quoted above. But at the end of tractate Ta'anit (31a), whoever does not rise from the fifteenth of Av onward, [it applies], "whoever adds, life is added to him, whoever does not add, is gathered in" — and Rashi explains: from here on, from the fifteenth of Av onward, whoever adds nights to days to occupy himself with Torah, life is added to his life; whoever does not add to his occupation with Torah, his mother will bury him — meaning, he will die before his time — so far his words. Some have given a mnemonic for this: "my lying-down until my rising, lie down" — meaning, from Shavuot until the Ninth of Av, lie down, for the nights are short; and from "my rising" until "my lying-down," rise. But the essential thing is to fulfill the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, particularly one who wishes to sanctify himself.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:129: Upon rising at midnight, it is fitting that he suffer in sympathy with the suffering of the Shechinah, and weep and lament over the destroyed Temple and the profaned Name, and finally over his own sins, which have lengthened the exile of the Shechinah — for it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayakhel 196a) that at midnight the Holy One, blessed be He, remembers Israel who are in exile and the destruction of His House, and so on; and then the souls of the righteous return to their bodies, and the angels say to them, "Behold, bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord," and so on. And midnight is a time of favor, as is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Terumah 173b), fitting for prayer that the Holy One, blessed be He, forgive his sins and that He return him in repentance.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:130: Afterward he should rise to occupy himself with Torah, and put on his clothes, and prepare himself to meet his God. So it says in the Zohar (Parashat Noach 72a), in these words: Rabbi Yehudah rose one night to study Torah in the guest-house in the town of Machseya, and there was a certain Jew there. He said to him, "How can this matter be, for the foundation stone..." and so on. Rabbi Yehudah did not turn his head toward him; he opened and said, "Prepare to meet your God, O Israel" (Amos 4:12), and it is written, "Take heed and listen, O Israel" (Deuteronomy 27:9) — words of Torah require intention, and words of Torah require that one be prepared together in body and will. That Jew arose, dressed, and sat down beside Rabbi Yehudah, and said, "Fortunate are you, righteous ones, who occupy yourselves with Torah day and night." Rabbi Yehudah said to him, "Now that you have prepared yourself, tell me your words, so that we may join together, for words of Torah require the rectification of body and heart together, and if not, I would as well have lain in my bed and spoken words in my heart." [The Jew answered:] "But have we not learned that even one who sits and studies Torah alone, the Shechinah joins with him? And is the Shechinah not here, while I lie in my bed [it would make no difference]?" [Rabbi Yehudah replied:] "Not only that, but purity is required, and further, whoever rises to occupy himself with Torah from midnight, when the north wind stirs at midnight, the Holy One, blessed be He, comes to delight with the righteous in the Garden of Eden, and He and all the righteous in the Garden of Eden listen to him, and listen to those words that go forth from his mouth; and if the Holy One, blessed be He, and all the righteous delight in hearing words of Torah at this hour, should I then lie in my bed?" — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:131: Upon rising he should occupy himself with the Oral Torah or with Mishnah. So the Targum renders the verse (Lamentations 2:19), "Arise, cry out in the night": "Arise, O Shechinah of Israel, who dwells in exile, occupy yourself with Mishnah at night, for the Shechinah of the Lord dwells opposite you." And so it says in Yalkut, end of Parashat Ki Tisa (remez 406), on the verse, "and he was there with the Lord forty days and forty nights" (Exodus 34:28) — but is it not written, "and light dwells with Him" (Daniel 2:22), and "the brightness shall be as the light" (Habakkuk 3:4), and "even the darkness does not obscure from You" (Psalms 139:12)? From where did Moses know when it was day and when it was night? At the hour the Holy One, blessed be He, was teaching him Scripture, he knew it was day; and at the hour He was teaching him Mishnah, he knew it was night — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:132: It is good that he rise standing, as much as he can bear, so as not to fall asleep — for so King David, peace be upon him, used to do, as explained in the Zohar (Parashat Lech Lecha 82b), in these words: come and see, King David used to rise at midnight — for should you say he sat or lay in his bed and said songs and praises, [that is] not so; rather, as it is written, "At midnight I will rise to give thanks to You" (Psalms 119:62) — "I will rise," certainly, standing, to occupy himself with songs and praises of Torah — so far his words. It may be that the verse also intends this in saying "arise, cry out" — meaning rise while standing. At the very least, if he does not have the strength to stand from the start of the reading, if sleep comes upon him, he should rise standing, for the essential thing is to bind night to day through occupation with Torah, as explained above.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:133: Likewise he should read his studies aloud, and thereby benefit in that he not fall asleep, and not forget it, as it is said, "for they are life to those who find them" (Proverbs 4:22, cf. Eruvin 54a). Regarding the greatness of raising one's voice while studying, it is elaborated in the Zohar (Parashat Shemini 39b) on the verse, "and your palate like the best wine, that goes down smoothly for my beloved" (Song of Songs 7:10) — see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:134: The general summary of all this is: whoever wishes to persist in this practice should strive in his deeds to acquire the neshamah, for it is said in the Zohar (Parashat Vayikra 25a) that whoever merits the neshamah is the one who strengthens himself like a lion in the study of Torah from midnight until morning, the reason being that the neshamah gives him strength. And we have already explained above (ch. 4) that the neshamah is acquired through occupation with Torah, and also through the purification of thoughts. It is also explained in the Tikkunim (113b) that penitents merit an additional neshamah every day, and therefore it should not be difficult for a penitent to rise at midnight, since the neshamah comes to him from a place called "strength" (koach).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:135: Also among the things needed to acquire this quality is that a person sanctify himself properly during the day, and purify his thoughts, and occupy himself with Torah to give satisfaction to his Creator and not for any worldly matter — by this he removes his nefesh from mere "doing" (asiyah) and attaches himself to holiness, and by this he will merit the neshamah. Now we have already learned, according to what we explained in the preceding chapters (ch. 4) through the statements of Rashbi, peace be upon him, that the acquisition of the neshamah is through occupation with Torah and purification of thoughts; and in the Zohar (Parashat Terumah 141b) it is explained that through the neshamah the Shechinah is aroused toward unification, in these words, regarding the neshamah: and this is for whose sake the lamp is lit, to shine above; and it says, by this it is comprised, whoever is comprised, and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:136: Now, when a person is engaged in mere "doing" and does not intend toward the One before whom he stands, whose glory fills the whole earth, he is [merely] physical and in "doing," and has no neshamah. So too regarding his eating and his blessings: if he blesses calmly and deliberately, and intends to give praise to his Maker, who is always before him — and this is the intent of "Blessed are You," according to the plain sense — and does not toss the blessing from his mouth hastily; and likewise in his eating, that he eats as one who eats before the King, and intends in his eating as is explained in its place — by this he is removed from materiality and sanctifies his soul with the supernal spirituality, and he merits the neshamah, and then the Shechinah rests within him; and since he is at the level of "living," sleep will not overpower him. But whoever is physical in his ways is [merely] in "doing," and sleep, which is death, will overpower him — would that he merit even the ruach.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:137: The second matter that causes the holiness of thought is a person's conducting himself properly during the six working days, as will be explained, so that on the day of Shabbat he receive the holiness of Shabbat, and Shabbat find in him a receptacle where its holiness may rest. Concerning this the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded us in the Ten Commandments, "Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it. Six days shall you labor and do all your work, and the seventh day is a Sabbath..." (Exodus 20:8-10), and its explanation is as we explained above in this Gate, chapter 2, that all the days nurse from the day of Shabbat, as we established necessarily there; and there we quoted their statement, of blessed memory (Mechilta, Parashat Yitro), that "Remember the Sabbath day" means that you should count for the sake of Shabbat, as explained there. The intent is that the holiness of Shabbat is a very supernal holiness, and it is impossible for a person to attain it because he is clothed in the six weekdays, over which the thirty-nine labors rule, and so on, as we elaborated there. Therefore he must sanctify himself every day with the holiness of Shabbat, so that when the day of Shabbat comes he will be able to receive its holiness.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:138: It is like the parable of a person who is in darkness — if he goes out into the light and receives the full force of the sun's light, it will darken his eyes and he will not enjoy the sweetness of its light. As the verse says, "and let us know, let us pursue the knowledge of the Lord; His going forth is prepared as the morning" (Hosea 6:3) — the light of dawn shines little by little. So the light of the holiness of Shabbat is a supernal holiness from Atzilut, shining from the Holy Ancient One, as Rashbi explains (Parashat Yitro 89a), as we elaborated there — and who could receive that great holiness [all at once]?
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:139: It is also like a garment upon which stains from oil or the like have fallen — if it is not washed and cleaned properly, it cannot receive any dye. So too whoever comes to receive the light of Shabbat while filthy, his soul soiled with the stains of his sins, the light of the supernal neshamah will not rest upon him, for he has no place to rest. Therefore one must remember Shabbat from the first day of the week, so that every single day he sanctify himself, until, when the holiness of Shabbat comes, the person is already accustomed to it, and it finds a prepared throne to rest upon.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:140: This is what it means by "Remember the Sabbath day" — the word "remember" is in the infinitive [imperative], for one must always remember the holiness of the Sabbath day in order to sanctify it, meaning so that you can sanctify it and receive its holiness, in such a way that when the day of Shabbat comes, it will shine upon all the days with force, since all the days will have been properly rectified and included in the middle point. But if the days are not rectified, so that a blemish is found in them, God forbid, Shabbat will not shine upon them from their own side, since they cannot receive its light — and all this is because of the soul of this person who blemishes, [showing] that he will not receive that illumination because he did not rectify. Thus this poor person is found lacking in two things: he lacks, on the Sabbath day, the holiness of Shabbat, and he lacks, in the six coming days, that the days of the past week did not properly receive the light of Shabbat, so that they might shine in the coming week as they should.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:141: Therefore it is proper, on the sixth day, to return in complete repentance and confess all that one has blemished in the six days, in order to properly receive the light of Shabbat as explained. It may be for this intention that a certain Rabbi used to fast every Sabbath eve. And in saying "the light of Shabbat," the intent is the additional soul (neshamah yeteirah), which each person receives according to the merit of his deeds during the six working days.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:142: Therefore the verse says, "Six days shall you labor..." (Exodus 20:9), meaning that in order to be able to receive the holiness of Shabbat, you must labor for six days — that is, you must be at the level of a servant. The conditions a servant is obligated to labor for his master, Rashbi, peace be upon him, explains in his commentary, printed at the end of Parashat Behar Sinai (111b), on the verse, "for the children of Israel are servants to Me" (Leviticus 25:55) — and we shall not quote all of his words at length, but the essence of his words is that within [the category of] "servant" there are two aspects: prayer, called "service" (avodah), is included, as they said (Ta'anit 2a), "what is the service of the heart? This is prayer"; and also included is serving the Holy One, blessed be He, with every kind of service, which are the commandments, like a servant serving his master because he is commanded to serve him. Included in this — although Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai did not write it there — as is written in Chovot HaLevavot (Gate of the Service of God, ch. 5): among the conditions of a servant is to be careful not to do anything against his master's will — this is the negative aspect, and he elaborates at length on the conditions of a servant in his explanation there — see there. The second aspect of "servant" is occupation with Torah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:143: In each of these one must combine both the aspect of "son" and "servant," for Israel are called "servants," as it is said, "for the children of Israel are servants to Me" (Leviticus 25:55), and are called "sons," as it is said, "You are children to the Lord your God" (Deuteronomy 14:1).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:144: Regarding prayer, one must be both servant and son — servant, to rectify what pertains from the Shechinah downward, in the lower worlds, and to unify Atzilut, from where they are called "sons." And whoever knows what Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, peace be upon him, explains in Parashat Pekudei, regarding the order of the chambers in the blessings of the Shema and the Amidah, will see that everything is done as one, servant and son. Regarding occupation with Torah, it says that when a person does not know and recognize his Maker except according to the plain sense, he is called, in general, "servant"; and so it is explained in the Tikkunim (Tikkunei Zohar Chadash 106b), that the six orders of the Mishnah are in Metatron, called "servant," and from there come the impure and the pure, and so on, as explained above in chapter 2. And when he is a "son," that is, when he knows the secrets of the Torah that are in Atzilut, like a son searching through his father's treasures, he is called "son" — this is the sum of his words there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:145: And in Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Mishpatim 115a) they explain the reason that one who occupies himself with Torah is called "servant," saying, in these words, on "if you buy a Hebrew servant, six years he shall serve" (Exodus 21:2): what is his acquisition? Rather, in the secrets of the Torah, Metatron is "a servant of the Lord," comprising six sides, corresponding to the six orders of the Mishnah; and through them a person must serve his Master, becoming a servant sold, "the acquisition of his money" — for money is the right [side] of Abraham, Chesed, his level; the Torah was given from there, and whoever occupies himself with it in order to merit the World to Come is called "the acquisition of his money" — the world of longing (kisufa) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:146: It further says there two particulars in which a person is called "servant": one, in tefillin — it says that he is His servant, with the yoke of tefillin on his head, and his ear is a strap, opened to hear the recitation of the Shema, [reading] "shema" (hear) in every language you hear. The second aspect, in prayer — as they said, of blessed memory (Berachot 34a), that the first three [blessings of the Amidah] are like a servant arranging his master's praises, and so on, and the last three are like a servant who has received a stipend from his master, and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:147: Now, for all these aspects the verse alludes in saying "six days shall you labor" — that when the days are rectified in these aspects, they become a throne to receive the light of Shabbat.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:148: Now it is fitting to know where in the verse the aspect of "son" is alluded to, according to the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, who says that a person must always be servant and son together, whether in prayer or in Torah. One might say it is alluded to in the verse, "Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it, six days..." — and it is known that the day of Shabbat, which is the light of Atzilut, is the aspect of "son"; and we have already said that "remember" is in the infinitive [imperative] — one must always remember the aspect of "son," which is the day of Shabbat, even during the six days, which is the mystery of "servant" — besides the day of Shabbat itself, which is entirely "unto the Lord your God" (Exodus 20:10). The prayer of the day of Shabbat is not like the prayer of the weekdays, and the occupation with Torah on the day of Shabbat is not like its occupation on the weekdays — for on the weekdays one intends the six orders of the Mishnah within Metatron, whereas on the day of Shabbat one intends them within the six extremities in Atzilut, where their source is, as explained in the Tikkunim (Tikkunei Zohar Chadash 106b).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:149: All the holinesses practiced on the day of Shabbat — the holiness of thought, the holiness of speech, and humility, which we explained above and in chapter 2 — one is obligated to practice on the weekdays too, so that when the day of Shabbat comes, he will be able to properly receive the light of the additional soul. This is likewise understood from the words of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, peace be upon him, in the Tikkunim (22b), in these words: for at the time the Shechinah is in exile it is said of her, "the dove found no rest" (Genesis 8:9), except on Shabbat and festivals, and at that time she is united with her husband, and how many additional souls descend with her to dwell in Israel — this is what is written, "and the children of Israel shall keep the Sabbath, to observe the Sabbath throughout their generations" (Exodus 31:16). Fortunate is he who prepares for her a pleasant dwelling in his heart, and pleasant vessels in his limbs, and a pleasant wife in his neshamah, for whose sake the supernal Shechinah, who is the soul of all life, rests upon it — so far his words. Certainly "a pleasant dwelling in his heart" means the purification of the heart's thoughts from evil imaginings, and "pleasant vessels in his limbs" means that they not be blemished — and certainly this preparation is needed for all six days, just as it is needed for the sixth day; for if his limbs are blemished for six days, what he rectifies on the sixth day will not suffice against what he blemished during the rest of the week's days. And "a pleasant wife in his neshamah" refers to the neshamah that was not blemished during the six weekdays, and by this he merits the additional soul resting upon him — this is what it says, "for whose sake the supernal Shechinah, who is the soul of all life, rests upon it" — that from her comes the addition of extra souls. This is what was explained regarding "Remember the Sabbath day," being in the infinitive [imperative] — that always, during the six weekdays, one must remember the holiness of Shabbat and make these good preparations — "a pleasant dwelling," and so on — so that he may receive the light of Shabbat resting upon him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:150: Likewise, on the six days when the Shechinah unites with Torah scholars who occupy themselves with Torah (Parashat Kedoshim 81a), if they do not make these mentioned preparations for her, certainly she will not rest upon them, for she does not rest upon a blemished soul, as it is said, "whatever has a blemish shall not come near" (Leviticus 21:18). Therefore a person must always purify his thoughts and rectify his deeds, and make a pleasant dwelling in his heart — rectifying the heart in all the particulars we discussed above regarding the rectification of the heart, positively and negatively — and pleasant vessels in his limbs, that they not be blemished, and that they have beauty and loveliness through the fulfillment of the commandments. "A pleasant wife in his neshamah" — the essential rectification of the neshamah is through Torah and the intention of prayer, for the neshamah is from the world of thought, and its rectification, adornment, and beauty come through the unifications a person performs through his thought; through this she shines, and he will thereby benefit — for when the day of Shabbat comes, it will be easy for him to purify his thought.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:151: All the holinesses a person practices on the day of Shabbat will be easier for him to practice on the weekdays, because on the day of Shabbat all the days receive, each single day, a portion of those holinesses; it will not be difficult for a person to practice what he had not done — so that if he did not rectify anything during the six days of the week, and Shabbat comes and he contemplates repentance and wishes to practice all the holinesses customary on it, all the holinesses he practiced on Shabbat will benefit him, making it easy for him to draw those holinesses from the middle point to all the days. But if the root, which is the point, is not properly rectified, it will be difficult for him to rectify each and every day, to illuminate and sanctify it with the holiness of thought and speech and the like. Therefore, whoever comes to sanctify himself should first sanctify the six days for the reason explained; and if he comes to repent on Shabbat, not having remembered his Maker during the working days, he should rectify the Shabbat as prescribed. At the very least, on Sabbath eve, he should make "a pleasant dwelling in his heart" — at least [purifying] his thought from the vanities of this world, and think of what we explained in chapter 2 of this Gate, that Shabbat is a foretaste of the World to Come, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Avodah Zarah 3a), "Whoever toils on Sabbath eve shall eat on Shabbat," and so on. It is likewise fitting that a person say in his heart, after preparing the needs of Shabbat in eating and drinking, "And what have I prepared for the world that is entirely Shabbat?" Therefore it is fitting that on the sixth day he seclude himself part of the day to examine what he has done during the six days, so that he may repent, and by this the days will be included in the middle point, which is Shabbat, as explained there, and his neshamah will be made pleasant through the intention of prayer as explained, and his limbs pleasant and rectified through at least contemplating repentance — and by this there will be a preparation for the additional soul to rest upon him, so that he may repent afterward.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:152: We have discussed, in general, the rectification of the working days that must be that of a servant, and the general aspect of the day of Shabbat. But there are further preparations proper to make on the sixth day to receive Shabbat, and preparations proper to make on Shabbat itself, some of which are explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayakhel 204a).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:153: The essential thing a person must do on the sixth day, in his body, to acquire the holiness of Shabbat and the additional soul, is immersion in forty se'ah [of water], in order to remove the garment of the weekday spirit and don the spirit of the holiness of Shabbat, which is the spirit that blows from the Ancient One — for which immersion is needed, and perhaps, through all this, that holy spirit will rest upon him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:154: Among these [preparations] is repentance, in thought and deed; the general rule is that alacrity, cleanliness, and purity all must be done on Sabbath eve, so that afterward the holiness — the holiness of Shabbat — may rest; and through these preparations there will be a pleasant dwelling in his heart, pleasant limbs, and a pleasant neshamah. And if these are lacking, God forbid, there is no rectification at all, and holiness finds no place to rest. He will benefit from this in that, since the holiness of Shabbat rests upon him properly, it will bring him to humility, fear of sin, piety, and holy spirit, as mentioned in the passage of Rabbi Pinchas (Avodah Zarah 20b) — for what causes a person not to be humble, fearing sin, pious, with his inclination overpowering him? It is because he lacks a neshamah that would overpower his inclination; and once a holy neshamah comes to him, it will certainly overpower it, and he will be humble, fearing sin, and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:155: According to the words of the Zohar in Parashat Vayakhel (204a), it seems to me that after immersing, it is forbidden for him to engage in performing labor, except in preparing the needs of Shabbat. It is correct that after the immersion he should occupy himself with Torah until he receives the Sabbath, for the immersion is almost like receiving the Sabbath, and this is its wording there: when Shabbat enters, the holy people must wash themselves from the contact of the weekday. Why? Because on the weekday a different spirit goes and roams and rests upon the people, and when a person wishes to leave that spirit and enter into another, holy, supernal spirit, he must wash himself so that that holy, supernal spirit may rest upon him — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:156: Among the things needed for the holiness of thought, the essential one is the primary fear that we explained in the Gate of Awe, chapter 1 — that a person should fear his Master, who is great and rules, the root and source of all worlds (Introduction to the Zohar 11b). And it is explained at the end of chapter 1 that a great fear should be drawn to a person from considering the Cause of all Causes, blessed and exalted be He, who is the root and sustenance of all the worlds, without whose flow they would have no existence; and included in this is the person, who is a small world, whom the Holy One, blessed be He, gives life through His flow — and if He were to gather His spirit and His soul to Himself, all flesh would perish together (Job 34:14-15); and concerning the Cause of all it is said, "and You give life to them all" (Nehemiah 9:6), as they explained, of blessed memory, "and You give life" and "You bring into being," and so on. And when a person stands in prayer or is occupied with Torah, and remembers that he stands before the Cause of all Causes, who is the root of all roots, and upon Him depends the root of the life of his soul, he should be embarrassed to think of anything else but what he is speaking before Him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:157: We mention this matter in the Musaf prayer of Rosh Hashanah, "You remember the deeds of the world, and consider all the creatures of old..." and my teacher, peace be upon him, explained, in explaining the prayer regarding what it says, "before You are revealed all hidden things and the multitude of secrets since the beginning" — that these are the mystery of the supernal, hidden "brightnesses" (tzachtzachot) in the root of all roots, through which all created things are portrayed all at once, in a single instant, and through those roots He provides for them, and His providence does not divide into the particulars of the lower ones, except that through those who are unified with Him, He bestows flow upon them and provides for them. The reality of these roots is revealed in Keter, [called] "primordial light, bright light, polished light," as is explained in the Tikkunim (135b), and my teacher, peace be upon him, explains in Pardes Rimonim, Sha'ar HaTzachtzachot (Gate 11, ch. 7), that the reality of these three lights corresponds to the three Yods in the Name Sag (Samech-Gimel, i.e. Yod-Vav-Dalet Heh-Yod Vav-Yod-Vav Heh-Yod), Yod-Kai Vav-Kai, and there is an allusion in the Tikkunim (there, and 115b).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:158: Further, in the Tikkunim in manuscript (Tikkunei Zohar Chadash 100a), it explains that the reality of these three Yods is the root of nefesh, ruach, and neshamah, in these words: fortunate is he who directs three prayers toward Him, in the three points of the segulah, from which are drawn three drops of the three supernal brains — for when semen is drawn from a person, those drops drawn from him are of the best of the best, of the finest of the brain; likewise, when the Holy One, blessed be He, causes to descend into a person the three bonds — neshamah, ruach, and nefesh — He gives them from the best of the best, from the three Yods of the segulah alluded to in the Name Yod-Kai Vav-Kai; and therefore it says of them, "and you the Lord has chosen to be for Him a treasured people (am segulah)" (Deuteronomy 14:2) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:159: When a person considers that his neshamah, ruach, and nefesh are rooted above, it is fitting that he purify his thoughts and be embarrassed to think of anything that is not His service, blessed be He — all the more so to speak or do anything against His will, since everything is revealed before Him, as King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 139:1-4), "O Lord, You have searched me and known me. You know my sitting down and my rising up, You understand my thought from afar... For there is not a word on my tongue, but, lo, O Lord, You know it altogether" — and as he elaborates afterward regarding [divine] providence, "Where shall I go from Your spirit...? If I ascend to heaven, You are there..."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:160: Know that all these aforementioned aspects regarding the root and source of all worlds are all revealed through the last attribute, as Rashbi says in this passage (Introduction to the Zohar 11b), "and to set his will on that level called awe (yirah)" — for all these aspects are grasped through it, and His providence, blessed be He, toward us is through this attribute, for it is the seal of the whole supernal Atzilut, and in it is the form of our souls, as we elaborated in the Gate of Awe, chapter 9, and through it the greatness and dominion of the supernal Emanator is revealed, as we explained in the Gate of Awe, chapter 1. This aspect of spiritual awe is what Rashbi, peace be upon him, warns us of several times: "voice and speech in awe and love" (Tikkunei Zohar 132a); "a commandment in awe and love" (Tikkunei Zohar 50a), and many similar phrases — the intent being that a person should know before whom he stands, and whom he serves and performs a commandment for, or occupies himself with Torah for, and not perform the commandment as a rote habit of men, and likewise regarding prayer and Torah study, but rather should be attached to his Maker as is fitting.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:161: From this awe, a person is drawn to humility of soul, to make himself small before the greatness of his Creator; and it is impossible for a person's soul to cleave to his God and draw holiness upon himself unless he subdues his soul before Him and considers himself as nothing compared to His greatness and all His goodness toward him. So Rashbi, peace be upon him, explains (Zohar Parashat Yitro 69a), in these words: because a supernal matter, whether of holiness or of the Other Side, cannot be drawn down from above by a person, or brought near to him, without awe — he must direct his heart and will with awe and a broken heart, and then the supernal spirit and the needed will shall be drawn down below; but if he does not set his heart and will with awe toward that side, his will cannot become attached to it — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:162: When a person wishes to cleave to his Master while occupied with Torah or prayer, he should first consider the aforementioned awe and subdue himself, and then the Holy One, blessed be He, will be found with him, and he will not be able to separate from Him easily — for the Holy One, blessed be He, in Himself, is always present and available, but on the person's side, from his own self and soul, and the kelipot that separate between him and his God, time is needed until he subdues himself and separates the kelipah from himself and cleaves to holiness.
